clue.text: Thinking comic has forgotten introduction

indicators.note: the comic word loses its opening letter, the introduction it has forgotten

parts.note: something comic is amusing, funny

explanation.surface: A comedian has lost the opening line of their routine and stands there pondering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has forgotten introduction' drops the first letter, A, from AMUSING.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: musing is quiet reflective pondering, the act of mulling something over.

clue.text: Suggestion mother should ring old detectives up

indicators.note: mother forms a ring around the other letters

parts.note: mum is mother

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the police detectives

explanation.surface: A hint that Mum ought to phone the old detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads the detectives backwards in this down clue; 'should ring' means mother goes round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small amount, a trace or hint, so a suggestion of something.

clue.text: Shelter in extremes of severest winter weather

indicators.note: the shelter word sits in between the two end letters
extremes of means the first and last letters of severest

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind

explanation.surface: Taking cover from the harshest winter conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes of' gives S and T from 'severest'; LEE goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleet is a mixture of rain and snow or ice pellets, typical cold-season precipitation.

clue.text: No way alcoholic drink is a remedy against ills

parts.note: St is short for street, a way
rum is an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Absolutely not: booze is no cure for what ails you.
explanation.walkthrough: ST, short for street, stands for 'way'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack medicine or pet scheme claimed to cure all ills.

clue.text: Roman soldiers take position, namely round Poland

parts.note: to man a post is to take up position at it

indicators.note: the letters for namely go around those for Poland

parts.note: i.e. (id est) means namely
PL is the international code for Poland

explanation.surface: A military order: occupy your post, specifically surrounding Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take position' is the verb 'man', as in staffing a post; 'round' puts the namely letters around Poland's code.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniple was a subdivision of a Roman legion, a unit of around a hundred or more troops.

clue.text: Undergraduates mustn't read set works without introduction from university

indicators.note: works as a verb means operates on or processes, so the letters are reworked
introduction from means the opening letter of university

explanation.surface: Students must not study the set texts unless introduced by their university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' rearranges MUSTNT READ SET together with U, the opening of 'university' ('introduction from'); 'without' places that U alongside, outside the other words.
explanation.definitionFit: Mature students are adults who begin a degree course later in life, a kind of undergraduate.

clue.text: So-called TV cook claiming turnover not good ultimately

indicators.note: turnover means the letters are turned over, read upwards
not good ultimately says the closing letter for good is dropped

parts.note: alleging means claiming

explanation.surface: A television chef's name, said to belong to someone who supposedly can't make a decent pastry turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not good ultimately' drops the final G from ALLEGING, leaving ALLEGIN; 'turnover' reads it upwards. Nigella Lawson is a British TV cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigella Lawson is a celebrated British television cook, widely known by her first name alone.

clue.text: Beg new worker to fill post

indicators.note: the new worker fills the post, sitting inside it

parts.note: a pale is a fence post or stake
a hand is a worker, a labourer

explanation.surface: Pleading for a fresh recruit to take up a vacant job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' is a stake (PALE), not a job; 'to fill' puts NHAND inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to panhandle is to beg in the street, chiefly American usage.

clue.text: To begin with, eggs are somewhat traditional, eaten regularly now?

indicators.note: to begin with points to the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Seasonal chocolate eggs are a fairly established treat, eaten often at this time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To begin with' takes the initials of six words. The question-mark definition 'now?' works because the puzzle appeared at Easter time.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle was published during the spring festival, so the current time is that Christian feast.

clue.text: Group of witches meeting round wood somewhere in London

parts.note: a coven is a gathering of witches

indicators.note: the meeting goes round the wood, enclosing it

parts.note: a tryst is a secret meeting
a tree is a source of wood

explanation.surface: A coven gathers around a tree in the forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' means the meeting encloses the wood. Coventry Street runs near Leicester Square in London's West End.
explanation.definitionFit: Coventry Street is a street in central London near Piccadilly Circus, so a place there.

clue.text: Formal attire ultimately associated with Socrates? Wrong

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of associated
wrong signals the name Socrates set out in a wrong order

explanation.surface: Was the Greek philosopher ever really linked with formal clothes? Surely not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives D, the end of 'associated'; 'Wrong' rearranges SOCRATES as RESSCOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress coat is a man's tailcoat worn for formal evening occasions, so it is formal wear.

clue.text: Class, say, backed by student group

indicators.note: backed tells us the abbreviation for say is turned backwards

parts.note: e.g. (for example) means say
the NUS is the National Union of Students, the UK student body

explanation.surface: A class, for example, supported by the students' union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns EG into GE. The NUS is the National Union of Students in the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: In biological taxonomy a genus is a category or kind, so a class in the general sense.

clue.text: Exclusive set of Biblical books the Virgin queen stored in church

indicators.note: the books and queen are kept inside the church letters, like goods stored

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
OT is the Old Testament, a set of Biblical books
Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen, is ER I (Elizabeth Regina the First)

explanation.surface: A list of scriptures and a royal portrait kept in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth I was called the Virgin Queen, her royal cipher ER plus the numeral I; 'stored in' puts the books and queen inside the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small, select circle of people who keep to themselves, an exclusive group.

clue.text: Issue of film about US general swallowing arsenic

parts.note: re means about, concerning

indicators.note: the general takes the arsenic inside him, swallowing it

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War
As is the chemical symbol for arsenic

explanation.surface: A war film about an American general who is poisoned with arsenic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowing' puts the arsenic symbol inside the general, giving LEASE; Robert E. Lee led the Confederate army.
explanation.definitionFit: When a film comes out in cinemas its distribution or issue is called its release.

clue.text: Enthusiastic amateur met with American and Arabs, avoiding one museum

parts.note: mad about something means very enthusiastic

indicators.note: avoiding one means the Arabs lose the letter for one

parts.note: Saudis are Arabs from Saudi Arabia
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A keen hobbyist meets an American and some Arabs, but steers clear of one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding' takes I (one) out of SAUDIS. Madame Tussauds is the London waxworks museum.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame Tussauds is the famous waxwork museum in London, an instance of a museum.

clue.text: Chocolate sweets, ice cream and a hot cake?

parts.note: chocolate drops are small sweets
a cone is an ice cream cornet

explanation.surface: A shopping list of treats: chocolates, an ice cream and something warm from the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: A drop scone is a small thick pancake cooked on a griddle and eaten warm.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop scone (Scotch pancake) is a griddle cake served warm, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Brother I sense buys rubbish: such suspicious behaviour

parts.note: a monk is a brother in a religious order

indicators.note: rubbish as a verb means to trash, so these words are scrambled

explanation.surface: A friar who senses that a purchase is junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbish' is a verb here, to trash, and works on the three words I SENSE BUYS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: monkey business is mischievous or underhand conduct, behaviour that looks dodgy.

clue.text: On a high after joints in party?

indicators.note: after places the high word following the joints

parts.note: knees are joints
up means in high spirits

explanation.surface: Feeling elated after smoking joints at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joints' means body joints, not cannabis. A knees-up is a lively British party with dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: Knees-up is British slang for a boisterous party or celebration.

clue.text: How to cause anger — smoke in church

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: to make someone very angry, enrage them
the noun sense: fragrant smoke from burning resin used in religious ritual

explanation.surface: Bothering a congregation by filling the church with smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: in-SENSE for anger, IN-sense for the smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: One spelling serves both the verb for enraging and the noun for aromatic ceremonial smoke.

clue.text: Major roads going north, crossing motorway

indicators.note: the roads cross over the motorway, enclosing it
in a down clue going north means the letters read upwards

parts.note: lanes are roads
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: Main roads heading north that pass over a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going north' makes SENAL in this down clue; 'crossing' sets the motorway, the M1 from London northwards, in the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Seminal means highly influential, of major importance in shaping later developments.

clue.text: Warning — snooker cue's useless with this

definitions.meaning: a confidential advance alert, as given to police
read as two words: a cue whose end piece has come away is no good

explanation.walkthrough: A snooker cue has a leather tip; with the tip off it cannot strike the ball properly.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip-off is a private piece of advance information, often warning of danger or crime.

clue.text: Examine fashionable glasses, half-complete

parts.note: in means fashionable, trendy

indicators.note: only half of the word for glasses is finished, its first five letters

parts.note: spectacles are glasses

explanation.surface: Look over some trendy eyewear that is only half made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-complete' keeps SPECT, the first half of SPECTACLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to inspect is to scrutinise something closely, looking it over carefully.

clue.text: Class should be entered in new exam, I shout

indicators.note: the class letters are entered inside the rearranged exam letters
new signals a fresh arrangement of exam and I

parts.note: CL is an abbreviation for class

explanation.surface: A student cries out that their class should sit a new exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges the exam letters and I as EXAIM; 'should be entered in' puts the class abbreviation inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to exclaim is to cry out suddenly, to call loudly.

clue.text: Burning a tree on 4th of November

parts.note: a fir is a tree

indicators.note: 4th of points to the fourth letter of November

explanation.surface: A tree set alight on Bonfire Night in early November.
explanation.walkthrough: '4th of' picks E from 'November'. The surface hints at Bonfire Night, 5 November, when Britain lights bonfires.
explanation.definitionFit: Afire means on fire, ablaze.

clue.text: Silver coins, round, sloven tossed back

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: the word for a sloven is thrown back, reading from right to left

parts.note: a slob is a sloven, an untidy lazy person

explanation.surface: A scruffy layabout flips round silver coins over his shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossed back' turns SLOB into BOLS.
explanation.definitionFit: The obol was a small silver coin of ancient Greece, worth a sixth of a drachma.

clue.text: Wife no longer has stress, finding extra house room?

parts.note: an ex is a former wife
tension is stress

explanation.surface: Divorced and free of strain, someone discovers spare space at home.
explanation.walkthrough: An ex is a former spouse, so 'Wife no longer' gives EX.
explanation.definitionFit: An extension is an added part built on to a house, giving extra rooms; the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: Surreptitiously tape most of film in old cinema

indicators.note: surreptitiously suggests something done slyly or out of order, so letters are mixed
most of drops the final letter of the word film

explanation.surface: Secretly recording a film on tape inside an old picture house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims FILM to FIL; 'Surreptitiously' rearranges TAPE plus FIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleapit is a British slang term for a shabby, run-down old picture house.

clue.text: Second of reviews penned by great art critic

indicators.note: the letter is enclosed, penned in, by the word for great

parts.note: swell means great, excellent

indicators.note: second of points to the second letter of reviews

explanation.surface: One of the reviews written by a great art critic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second of' takes E from 'reviews'; 'penned by' puts it inside SWELL. Brian Sewell was a celebrated London art critic.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Sewell was a well-known British art critic for the Evening Standard.
